title: SAP is reported to be weighing at least 10,000 job cuts as AI reshapes its software business. OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets and suppliers, Canada adds C$700 million to its AI compute fund and will now cover up to 80% of costs on Canadian-owned clouds, and Switzerland confirms its first AI-agent cyberattacks. Tencent open-sources DFly2 to speed up long agent runs.
summary: Bloomberg says SAP is weighing at least 10,000 job cuts, with product, engineering and sales in focus; SAP says no decisions have been made. OpenAI filed counterclaims accusing Apple of stealing trade secrets and pressuring suppliers, and Apple denies it. Canada’s AI Compute Access Fund reaches $1 billion and reimburses up to 80% of compute from sovereign providers and up to 50% from Canadian-based ones, with a first call for health and life sciences. Switzerland’s cyber agency reports its first attacks carried out with AI agents, and Microsoft details the ARTEX framework behind many of them. Tencent open-sourced DFly2, which it says gives up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
uncertainty: The SAP figure comes from unnamed sources via Bloomberg; SAP says no decisions have been made. OpenAI’s and Apple’s accounts are court filings and statements, not findings, and both sides deny the other’s claims. The Canadian rates are the program’s maximums, and the earlier 67% rate comes from BetaKit and The Logic. The Swiss agency’s notice gives no counts; the five attacks and four successes come from Reuters, and the agency’s own wording says compromise followed in every case it knows of. DFly2’s figures are self-reported by Tencent, measured on its chosen tasks, and the gain ranges from 3.9% to 81%.

stories.theme: SAP is reported to be weighing at least 10,000 job cuts as it reshapes its software business around AI
stories.changed: Bloomberg reported on 26 November that SAP, Germany’s largest software company, is preparing a plan to cut at least 10,000 positions as it reshapes its software business for the AI era, citing people familiar with the matter. CNBC, relaying the report, says all departments were asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus. SAP employs more than 110,000 people. SAP told CNBC that “no decisions have been made regarding any further measures” and that it does not comment on speculation. The report came as SAP flagged a cybersecurity attack, saying it found “no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.” In 2024 SAP removed around 10,000 positions through a programme that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining, and headcount later stayed relatively flat as it hired for new roles.
stories.matters: The departments named, product, engineering and sales, are the people who build and sell software. CNBC adds that other software firms have tied cuts to AI this year, and that US employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, about 20% of the total, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
stories.imply: Treat this as a signal, not a decision: SAP says nothing is settled and the figure comes from unnamed sources. But software and business-service teams should expect questions about which work needs a person and which can be handed to AI tools, and should have an answer ready.
uses: Managers: list the repeatable, rule-based tasks your team does each week, and mark which ones need judgement or a client relationship. That is the list you will be asked for.
Individual staff: write down the work where you check, fix or approve AI output; that is the part that is hard to replace and easy to show.
Hiring and training leads: if you retrain rather than lay off, as SAP mainly did in 2024, record what skills you are moving people towards.
stories.example: A sales-operations lead at a software reseller lists her team’s tasks: quote formatting and renewal reminders are repeatable and go to an AI assistant, while pricing exceptions and customer calls stay with people. She brings the list to her manager before the planning round, not after.
stories.audience: Staff and managers at software and business-service firms, HR and workforce planners, and anyone whose job involves sales, product or engineering support.
stories.watch: Whether SAP confirms a plan and a number, whether any cuts rely on voluntary departures as in 2024, and whether other software firms follow with AI-linked cuts.

source.title: CNBC: German software firm SAP is reportedly cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push, 27 November 2026
source.quote: The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful

stories.theme: OpenAI countersued Apple, accusing it of stealing trade secrets and pressuring hardware suppliers
stories.changed: On Friday 27 November OpenAI filed counterclaims in a California federal court against Apple, which sued OpenAI and former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July over alleged trade-secret misappropriation. OpenAI says Apple rehired a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months, and that in that time he gained access to specific information on a new device and to OpenAI’s hardware roadmap. It also says Apple discouraged hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices, and designed its employment practices to “trap” employees. OpenAI says 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far. Apple denies using the rehired employee to get OpenAI’s confidential information and denies trying to suppress competition, calling the counterclaims “a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit.” OpenAI and the two former Apple employees deny Apple’s allegations. These are claims in court filings, not findings.
stories.matters: The fight is about people and devices as much as models. OpenAI says it is building AI devices that could “outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf”, and the dispute shows how hiring, personal devices and supplier relationships are becoming legal issues in the race to build AI hardware.
stories.imply: Companies that hire from rivals, or lose staff to them, should expect closer scrutiny of what people carry between jobs. OpenAI’s filing also criticises Apple for asking staff to use personal devices and accounts for work and then blocking an orderly separation when they leave, which any employer with a bring-your-own-device policy should read as a warning.
uses: HR and legal teams: check your exit process for staff who use personal phones or accounts for work, and agree in writing what is returned or wiped.
Hiring managers: record what a new hire from a competitor is, and is not, allowed to bring or use.
Hardware startups: note which suppliers you depend on for key parts, and what happens if a larger rival leans on them.
stories.example: A start-up hires an engineer from a larger rival. HR gives him a one-page note on what he may not bring, asks him to confirm he has returned company files from his old job, and keeps the signed note on file.
stories.audience: HR, legal and operations leads, founders hiring from big companies, and consumer-hardware makers.
stories.watch: How the court handles the counterclaims, whether suppliers are drawn in, and whether other companies tighten rules for personal devices at work.

source.title: Reuters: OpenAI countersues Apple for stealing trade secrets, 27 November 2026
source.quote: Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place

stories.theme: Canada added C$700 million to its AI Compute Access Fund and will now cover up to 80% of compute bought from Canadian-owned clouds
stories.changed: On 26 November Canada’s AI minister Evan Solomon announced $700 million more for the AI Compute Access Fund, building on the first $300 million and bringing the total to $1 billion. The updated program guide says the fund covers up to 80% of eligible costs for cloud compute from sovereign providers, and up to 50% for Canadian-based providers. A sovereign provider must be incorporated in Canada, ultimately Canadian-owned and controlled, run its compute in Canada, and keep data processed and stored there; multinationals with a Canadian entity count as Canadian-based. Proposals must have eligible compute costs between $100,000 and $5 million, for projects ending by 31 March 2030. The first call is for health and life sciences. A statement of interest is due by 17 December 2026 and the full application by 4 January 2027, 11:59 pm Eastern time. BetaKit and The Logic report the earlier phase covered up to 67% when Canadian providers were used. The government also announced $52 million for 45 more companies from the first phase, bringing commitments to more than $118 million for 89 companies.
stories.matters: The subsidy depends on where the compute is bought. The same AI bill is reimbursed at a higher rate if the cloud company is Canadian-owned than if it is a foreign firm’s Canadian region. That changes who small AI firms in Canada buy from, and gives local cloud providers a price edge.
stories.imply: Governments are starting to pay for AI compute and to steer where it is bought. Canadian small and mid-sized firms working in health and life sciences should check eligibility now, and cloud buyers elsewhere should expect similar sovereignty conditions to attach to public money.
uses: Canadian health and life-science firms: read the program guide, check whether your yearly compute bill falls between $100,000 and $5 million, and submit the statement of interest by 17 December.
Finance leads: ask your cloud supplier whether it meets the sovereign test, since it changes the share you can claim.
Cloud providers: document ownership, data location and where processing happens, because the guide asks for contracts and proof.
stories.example: A Toronto medical-imaging start-up spends $400,000 a year on AI compute. It asks its provider for proof of Canadian ownership and data location, then files a statement of interest before 17 December.
stories.audience: Canadian small and medium-sized AI firms, especially in health and life sciences, plus cloud providers and their finance teams.
stories.watch: Which firms count as sovereign providers, the next sector calls after health, and whether other countries copy the idea.

source.title: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada: Program Guide, AI Compute Access Fund, updated 26 November 2026
source.quote: Cover up to 80% of your eligible costs for sovereign, cloud-based compute services.

stories.theme: Switzerland’s cyber agency confirmed its first attacks run by AI agents, and says the free tools behind them have almost doubled since October
stories.changed: Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC, also called BACS) said it has received its first reports of cyberattacks in Switzerland carried out with the help of an AI agent, hitting organisations and critical infrastructure operators in at least two sectors. Reuters reported five attacks in recent days, four of them successful, with three targeting critical infrastructure operators; broadcaster SRF said these were electricity, water and telecoms providers. The NCSC says the attackers used “Agentic Offensive Frameworks”, AI agents that search for weak points, pick attack tools, check the results and plan the next step. It says the number of internet-accessible agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI has almost doubled since October 2026. Microsoft Threat Intelligence said on 25 November that ARTEX, released in July as a penetration-testing framework, is now used by state-backed and criminal groups, and can move from scanning to privileged access in minutes. The NCSC advises patching internet-facing systems no later than 24 hours after release, using multi-factor authentication or passkeys, and limiting what is exposed.
stories.matters: These tools are free and widely available, so the main change is speed. The NCSC says such agents need only a fraction of the time a human would to find and use weak systems, which leaves less time to spot and stop an attack.
stories.imply: Slow patching and shared or easy passwords are now a bigger risk than before. Small firms that supply bigger ones are as exposed as the large targets, and security plans written for human-speed attackers need a second look.
uses: IT leads: list every system reachable from the internet and remove or restrict any that do not need to be.
Operations leads: set a rule that critical security updates are installed within 24 hours, and name who approves it.
Everyone: switch on multi-factor authentication or passkeys for email, VPN and other internet-facing logins.
stories.example: A water-meter supplier lists its remote-support portals and finds one that no one uses. It shuts that down, puts passkeys on the rest and sets a 24-hour patch rule.
stories.audience: IT and security teams, owners of small suppliers to utilities and large companies, and anyone who runs internet-facing systems.
stories.watch: Whether the NCSC or other national agencies publish counts and sectors, and whether more countries report attacks run by AI agents.

source.title: Swiss National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC/BACS): Cyberattacks involving AI agents, first confirmed cases in Switzerland, November 2026
source.quote: AI agents often require only a fraction of the time a human would need to locate such vulnerable systems and exploit existing vulnerabilities.

stories.theme: Tencent open-sourced DFly2, a helper that makes long, agent-style AI runs cheaper to serve, with up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
stories.changed: On 26 November Tencent’s Hunyuan team open-sourced DFly2, a speculative-decoding drafter. In plain terms, a small helper model guesses several words ahead and the big model checks them in one pass, so the output is the same but arrives faster. DFly2 reads the big model’s own memory (its KV cache) and its choice of which earlier text to look at, instead of keeping a separate copy, so the helper adds no extra memory and its cost stays flat at any context length. MarkTechPost reports Tencent’s figures: up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 64K context, compared with the DSpark helper at the same per-user speed, with 62% on a code task and 28% on short text. Tencent claims up to 4.2 times faster decoding on long agent tasks with its Hy4 flash model. The smallest gain was 3.9% on general tasks with Hy4 flash. MarkTechPost notes all numbers are self-reported by Tencent.
stories.matters: Long agent sessions are expensive because the model re-reads a lot of text. A helper that adds no memory and holds its cost at long context speeds up exactly the kind of runs coding agents produce, and it is open for teams that host their own models.
stories.imply: Teams that run their own open models can serve more users on the same hardware, or answer faster, without changing the big model. The gain varies by task and model, so test it on your own work before planning around Tencent’s best figure.
uses: Platform teams running DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash or Hy4 flash: benchmark DFly2 against your current helper on your real prompts.
Developers using agents with very long context: ask your host whether it supports a drafter like this.
Finance leads: ask engineers for measured cost per task before and after, not Tencent’s headline.
stories.example: An engineering team that runs Hy4 flash for code review agents tries DFly2 on last week’s long review jobs. It records time per job and cost on the same hardware, and compares with its current setup before deciding.
stories.audience: Teams that host open AI models, platform and infrastructure engineers, and technical leads who pay for long-context agent runs.
stories.watch: Independent benchmarks, support in common serving software, and the licences: MarkTechPost lists an AngelSpec License and the Tencent Hy License for Hy4 flash.

source.title: MarkTechPost: Tencent Open-Sources DFly2, Speculative Decoding That Reuses the Target’s Sparse KV Cache, 26 November 2026
source.quote: Up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 64K, at matched per-user speed.

signals.raw: CNBC, 27 Nov (Bloomberg, 26 Nov): SAP preparing plan to cut at least 10,000 positions as it reshapes software business for AI; all departments asked to identify cuts, product, engineering, sales in focus; 110,000+ employees; SAP statement: no decisions made on further measures, does not comment on speculation; SAP flagged cyberattack, no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data; 2024 programme ~10,000 positions mainly voluntary departures and retraining; WiseTech ~2,000 (Feb), Atlassian ~1,600 (Mar), Cloudflare 1,100+ (May); Challenger, Gray & Christmas 5 Nov: AI cited in 121,401 US job-cut announcements through Oct 2026, ~20%.

Reuters, 27 Nov: OpenAI counterclaims in California federal court vs Apple (Apple sued OpenAI, Tang Tan, Chang Liu in July). OpenAI: rehired ex-employee (six months at OpenAI) accessed device information and hardware roadmap; Apple discouraged suppliers; employment practices designed to trap employees; 400 employees left Apple for OpenAI. Apple denies, calls counterclaims transparent attempt to distract. OpenAI and employees deny Apple’s claims.

ISED Canada, 26 Nov: $700M expansion of AI Compute Access Fund (initial $300M, total $1B); program guide updated 26 Nov: up to 80% of eligible costs for sovereign cloud compute, up to 50% for Canadian-based; costs $100,000 to $5M; projects to 31 Mar 2030; first call health and life sciences; SOI by 17 Dec 2026, deadline 4 Jan 2027 11:59 pm ET; $52M to 45 more companies, total >$118M for 89. BetaKit and The Logic: previous rate 67%.

NCSC/BACS Switzerland notice: first reports of attacks with AI agents (Agentic Offensive Frameworks), organisations and critical infrastructure in at least two sectors; ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI accessible agents almost doubled since Oct 2026; recommendations: limit exposure, patch within 24 hours, MFA/passkeys, least privilege, monitor behaviour, pen tests. Reuters/CNA, 26 Nov: five attacks, four successful, three critical infrastructure operators (SRF: electricity, water, telecoms). Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 25 Nov: ARTEX (released July 2026) used by Storm-0940, Salt Typhoon and others; recon to privileged access in minutes.

MarkTechPost, 26 Nov; Tencent Hy on X, 26 Nov 12:22 UTC: DFly2 speculative-decoding drafter open-sourced; shares target KV cache and top-k selection; up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 64K vs DSpark at matched per-user speed (62% CodeSpan 64K, 28% short text); up to 4.2x on Hy4 flash agentic tasks; smallest gain 3.9% on Hy4 flash general; self-reported; AngelSpec License, Hy4 flash under Tencent Hy License.
